title: Brie-Style Gulmarg to Gruyère-Inspired Yeoor: The Indian Cheeses PM Modi Gifted the Swiss President
excerpt: The three Eleftheria Cheese varieties — Gulmarg, Konark and Yeoor — all international award-winners, were gifted to Guy Parmelin on October 5 alongside a Kashmiri walnut panel.
body:
• Prime Minister Narendra Modi gifted three award-winning Indian cheeses — Gulmarg, Konark and Yeoor, from Mumbai's Eleftheria Cheese — to Swiss President Guy Parmelin during his state visit to India on October 5.
  • Gulmarg is a heart-shaped Brie-style cheese that won Super Gold at the 2026 Mundial do Queijo do Brasil; Konark is a Tomme-style cheese that won Gold at the 2023 World Cheese Awards in Norway and Silver in Bern in 2025; Yeoor is a Gruyère-inspired mountain cheese aged eight to nine months.
  • The gift also included a Kashmiri walnut wood wall panel and, for Parmelin's wife, a Kutchi shawl and Sadeli box.
  • For food lovers: all three cheeses come from Mumbai-based artisanal producer Eleftheria Cheese, founded by Mausam Narang — and they are available to buy in India.

Switzerland is famous for its cheese. So when Prime Minister Narendra Modi sat down with Swiss President Guy Parmelin in New Delhi on October 5, he brought India’s own answer: three award-winning Indian cheeses — Gulmarg, Konark and Yeoor — from Mumbai-based artisanal producer Eleftheria Cheese.

The cheeses took centre stage alongside bilateral talks covering transportation technologies, mobility systems and infrastructure, as well as trade, investment, defence, nuclear energy and critical technologies during Parmelin’s three-day state visit — his first state visit to India.

Meet the three cheeses

Gulmarg is a Brie-style cheese with a snowy, velvety rind, aged two to three weeks. It is heart-shaped, soft and creamy, made from pasteurised cow’s milk, with an earthy, mushroom-like character. It won Super Gold at the 4th Mundial do Queijo do Brasil 2026 — the world cheese championship held in Brazil. Founder Mausam Narang suggests pairing it with hot honey, candied pistachios, fig or berry jam and sparkling white wine, or baking it until gooey for sourdough sandwiches and cheese platters.

Konark is a Tomme-style cheese whose distinctive wheel shape pays homage to the Konark Sun Temple chariot. Aged for two months, it develops a natural, rustic rind over a smooth, pale ivory interior with nutty, herbaceous notes and a tangy finish. It won Gold at the World Cheese Awards 2023 in Norway and Silver at the 2025 edition in Bern, Switzerland. An excellent melter, it suits fondue, gratins and grilled cheese.

Yeoor is a mountain-style cheese inspired by the Swiss Gruyère tradition, aged eight to nine months. Named after the Yeoor Hills bordering Sanjay Gandhi National Park near the creamery, it won Silver at the World Cheese Awards 2025 in Bern. Its rind is decorated with rose petals and fennel, giving it what its makers call an Indian-Alpine character, and its melting qualities make it suited to fondue and baked dishes.

Context: culinary diplomacy, Indian style

Food has long been Modi’s diplomatic instrument — from the state banquets to the curated gift hampers that travel with him. Choosing cheese for the president of Switzerland is a deliberate flex: it says India’s artisanal food sector can now compete on the home turf of the world’s most exacting cheese culture. The gesture also arrived with a Kashmiri walnut wood wall panel — hand-carved in deep relief, depicting landscapes, flora, horses and village life — and, for Parmelin’s wife, a Kutchi shawl and Sadeli box from Gujarat.

India’s specialty cheese scene has quietly matured over the past decade. Eleftheria, founded by Mausam Narang in Mumbai, is part of a wave of Indian cheesemakers adapting European styles — Brie, Tomme, Gruyère — while developing products with local character. The international medals suggest the adaptation is working.

What this means for you

You don’t need a state visit to taste them. Eleftheria’s cheeses are sold in India through specialty retailers, and the presidential spotlight is likely to push all three into wider distribution. For Diwali cheese boards — increasingly a thing in urban India and the diaspora — Gulmarg’s baked-Brie potential and Konark’s fondue-friendly melt are the practical picks.

Diaspora angle

For the diaspora, the story lands twice: as pride in an Indian product beating Europeans at their own game, and as a practical shopping list. Indian artisanal cheese is now export-grade; if your local Indian grocer stocks Eleftheria, this is the week to try it.
